title: What's at stake as Canada's top court ruling on Quebec secularism law looms
summary: Ahead of Friday's highly anticipated Supreme Court of Canada ruling on Quebec's controversial secularism law, which bars some public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, there is…

image.caption: Canada's top court says its decision on Quebec's secularism law will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET Friday. (Tom Hanson/Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal

Ahead of Friday's highly anticipated Supreme Court of Canada ruling on Quebec's controversial secularism law, which bars some public sector workers from wearing religious symbols on the job, there is optimism on both sides of the debate.
Friday's ruling on Bill 21 could establish key boundaries when it comes to fundamental rights
The big question now is whether the country's top court will rein in the use of the Constitution's notwithstanding clause.
Some legal observers say the decision could be studied by law students for generations to come, while others view it as a potential stepping stone toward lasting change rather than the final word.
"It will not be the end of the conversation on Friday," said Karine Millaire, a Université de Montréal law professor and lawyer who represents the International Commission of Jurists in the case.

"I would be very surprised if it would close all the doors and that it would answer all the questions," she said, noting the court is already scheduled to hear another notwithstanding clause challenge out of Saskatchewan in March.
That’s a fight about children's pronouns and names in Saskatchewan's schools, but here in Quebec, the debate is over the secularism law, known as Bill 21.
Canada's top court says its decision will be released at 9:45 a.m. ET Friday.
Why all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21
Ruling felt across Canada
The decision is expected to reverberate nationwide and could carry major political consequences as the Parti Québécois, which has vowed to take Bill 21 even further, now holds a minority government.
The law, which applies to teachers and police officers among others, was adopted in June 2019 by the Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government.
It quickly faced a constitutional challenge, with civil liberties groups arguing that the legislation discriminates against Muslim women who wear head coverings.

items: Supreme Court ruling on Quebec's secularism law coming on Nov. 27
6 key moments from the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec's secularism law

blocks.text: In April 2021, a Quebec Superior Court judge rendered a decision that described Bill 21 as a law that violates the basic rights of religious minorities in Quebec — but that those violations are permissible because the law invoked the Constitution's notwithstanding clause.
The notwithstanding clause allows governments, including provincial governments like Quebec, to temporarily shield laws from court challenges over fundamental rights violations.
In 2024, the Court of Appeal upheld most of the Superior Court's ruling and even overturned a previous exemption for English school boards.
Now, the notwithstanding clause is at the heart of the Supreme Court's upcoming decision, Millaire said.

While she doesn't expect the court to deliver a "black-or-white" ruling that either eliminates the notwithstanding clause or gives governments the power to override rights, she said the justices will have to weigh whether its use has limits — and whether courts can formally declare that a law violates fundamental rights even if the clause keeps it in force.

"At a minimum, people can expect to know if there is a violation of their rights — rights of many Quebecers,” Millaire said, noting that Quebec chose not to present evidence to justify the law, relying instead on the clause alone to shield it from scrutiny.
Both sides hopeful

Daniel Baril, president of the provincial secularism group Mouvement laïque québécois, said he is "reasonably optimistic" ahead of Friday's decision, pointing to a 2015 Supreme Court ruling his organization won against the City of Saguenay over prayer at city council meetings.

In that unanimous ruling, the court said the state must remain religiously neutral — a precedent Baril argues extends to public sector employees and forms the foundation of Bill 21. It means the law shouldn't even require the notwithstanding clause, he said.
"A unanimous ruling at the Supreme Court is very rare," Baril said in an interview Wednesday, noting Chief Justice Richard Wagner was a justice back then.
"He already signed off on that ruling, and today he is the chief justice. We hope he will have convinced the others."

items: Quebec’s secularism laws upended their lives. They fear what comes next could be worse

blocks.text: However, in that 2015 decision, the Supreme Court did not rule out the presence of religious symbols, because it decided to limit the scope of its investigation to prayer only.

On the other side of the debate, Stephen Brown, the CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims (NCCM), said he is also hopeful ahead of Friday's decision — but warned that the stakes extend far beyond Quebec, affecting the rights of millions of Canadians.
Stephen Brown, president of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, says the Supreme Court ruling extends far beyond Quebec. (Natalia Weichsel/CBC)
For Brown, the core question before the court is whether governments can unilaterally strip away fundamental Charter rights without justification or judicial oversight.
"Long story short: can politicians play wedge politics with the rights of Canadian citizens?" Brown said.

"If the answer to that question is yes, that is a massive problem for who we are as a country. Because if politicians can play wedge politics with our rights, we don't have rights — what we actually have are permissions."

items: Quebec Appeal Court Bill 21 ruling fuels debate on notwithstanding clause

blocks.text: Harini Sivalingam, director of the equality program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association (CCLA), said Friday's ruling will be one of the most consequential constitutional decisions in modern Canadian democracy.
With other provinces increasingly using or floating the notwithstanding clause on issues ranging from trans youth to homeless encampments, she said the stakes could not be higher.
"The implications extend far beyond Quebec and religious symbols," Sivalingam said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
